title: The 40-year arc
copy:
In 1987, Apple released a concept video called the Knowledge Navigator.

It showed a future where a conversational assistant knew you — your work, your calendar, your life — and just... handled things. Research, scheduling, the boring stuff. You talked, it did.

I was in my twenties. And I never stopped thinking about it.

In 1993 I built my own version for the Mac. It worked. People used it.

And now, 40 years after that concept video, I'm building it again — for today's world, with today's AI. The tech finally caught up to the idea.

The vision took 40 years. We're building it now.

More nuggets coming. This is going to be fun.

title: The Knowledge Navigator
copy:
People remember the Knowledge Navigator as a slick Apple concept video.

What stuck with me wasn’t the slickness. It was the premise: an assistant that knew enough about you to be genuinely useful. Not a search box. Not a command line. A colleague.

1987. No internet to speak of. The whole thing was fiction.

But it planted a question I’ve been carrying for almost four decades: what if your computer actually knew what you needed before you asked?

That’s the thread. Everything since has been following it. 📼

title: Rae Assist, 1993
copy:
So in 1993, I built one.

Rae Assist: a personal assistant for the Mac. It managed your day, your contacts, your information — the stuff a good assistant does. This was before “personal assistant” meant a voice in a speaker.

It was real software. Real users. One of them ran it on a PowerBook 160 in New York City and never forgot it.

I shelved it eventually. The world wasn’t ready, and honestly, neither was the tech. But I kept the idea.

Ideas are patient. They wait. 💾

title: The fall
copy:
Last fall, someone asked me if I’d ever revive Rae Assist.

I said no.

I meant it, too. It was a good memory, a good story. Some things belong to their era.

Then AI got good. Like, actually good — not demo good, but ‘this changes what software can be’ good.

And that old question came back: what if your computer actually knew what you needed before you asked?

So I called the person who asked last fall, and I said: things changed. I’m building it.

Never say never. Especially to your own ideas. 🍂

title: Penny's return
copy:
When I decided to rebuild Rae Assist, the first person I told was one of its original users.

She ran the 1993 version on her PowerBook 160. She's in New York, in entertainment, and she remembered it — the feel of having a machine that had your back.

She's now the first civilian tester of the new version.

There's something right about that. The first user is back. The circle closes, and a new one opens. 🙏

title: Why now
copy:
Why now? Fair question. The idea is 40 years old.

Because the missing piece was never the vision — it was the engine. In 1987 the Knowledge Navigator was a concept video. In 1993 my assistant was clever software running on a machine with a fraction of the power in your watch.

Today the models can actually understand what you mean, remember what matters, and do multi-step work. The idea didn’t change. The world caught up to it.

Forty years of waiting, and the last piece just clicked into place.

That’s why now. 🧩

title: What it is — a staff
copy:
Okay, so what am I actually building?

Not an app. A staff.

A buddy is the smallest unit of your staff: one slice of your life with a thread you can talk to, a memory that never forgets, and a homepage showing its current state. Money gets a buddy. Your calendar gets a buddy. Your car gets a buddy.

They’re all wired together, so anything you drop anywhere finds the right desk.

Less ‘app,’ more ‘person who never forgets and never sleeps.’

Over the next couple weeks I’ll introduce you to the staff, one buddy at a time. 🤝

title: The trojan horse
copy:
Where do you start when you’re building a whole staff?

With money. Everyone understands money.

So the first buddy out the door is Money Buddy. It knows your bills, your cash flow, your spending — and you just talk to it. ‘What bills do I have coming up?’ ‘Can I afford this trip?’ ‘Where’s all my money going?’

Not a ledger. A financial advisor that happens to live in your phone.

This week I’ll show you what it does. Each one of these is real — things I actually asked it. 🐴

title: Forgotten subscriptions
copy:
How much did you pay for a financial advisor to find your forgotten subscriptions?

I asked my money buddy: 'What subscriptions am I still paying for that I forgot about?'

It went through my transactions and came back with the list. The ones I'd forgotten. The ones quietly billing me every month for things I don't use.

A financial advisor charges $200+ an hour for that conversation.

I paid $0.

There's a tip jar. [link coming — tip jar being set up this week] 👻

title: Double-charged
copy:
‘Did I get double-charged for anything?’

That’s a question you ask a human — your accountant, your bookkeeper. Someone you’d pay.

I asked my money buddy instead. It checked. (It had, once. A streaming service. Caught it, killed it.)

The point isn’t the one charge. The point is there’s now someone watching — all the time, for free — who never gets tired and never forgets to look.

More of these coming. The money stories write themselves. 👀

title: The eyeglasses story
copy:
Real one from this month.

I told my money buddy: ‘Budget for two pairs of eyeglasses, about $700 a pair.’

It looked at my bills, my cash flow, my bank balance — and told me when I could buy them. Not a lecture. A plan.

That’s the difference between a ledger and an advisor. A ledger tells you what you spent. An advisor tells you what to do next.

How much did you pay for that advice? $0.

There’s a tip jar. [link coming — tip jar being set up this week] 👓

title: One picture
copy:
‘Show me where my money went this year in one picture.’

One sentence. One picture back. Ten months of spending, laid out so I could actually see it.

I’ve had budgeting apps for years. They show me charts I never look at. This is different — because I asked in words, like I’d ask a person, and got an answer I could use.

The best interface is still a conversation. We just finally have software that can hold up its end. 🖼️

title: The staff grows
copy:
Money Buddy is the first one out the door because everyone understands money.

But it’s not the only desk in the office.

There’s a buddy for your calendar, one for your health, one for your house, one for your car. One for the trip you’re planning. One for the party you’re throwing. Each one knows its slice of your life cold.

Over the next few weeks: meet the staff. One buddy at a time, one job it does, one real moment.

It’s a lot of someones. That’s the point. 🌱

title: The tip jar
copy:
So here’s the business model, all of it:

Everything I’ve shown you — the money buddy, the staff, all of it — I paid $0 for. I built it. It’s mine.

And there’s a tip jar.

No subscriptions. No pitch deck. No ‘freemium.’ If it helps you, toss something in the jar. If not, no hard feelings.

Software used to be something you bought once and owned. I kind of miss that. This is my version of it: built in the open, priced at whatever you think it’s worth.

The jar opens soon. 🫙
